## What is a linkage?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Links** are stiff bars. **Joints** (pins) let them turn.
- A **four-bar linkage** has four links:
  - the **ground** (it doesn't move)
  - the **crank** (we turn it)
  - the **coupler** (it joins the two sides)
  - the **rocker** (it swings)
- Turn the crank, and every other link moves in its own way.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Four-bar linkages are everywhere:**

- a car's windshield wipers
- your leg and a bike pedal
- an oil pump "nodding donkey"
- a folding chair
- a robot's gripper
:::
::::

## A four-bar linkage {#four-bar}

<iframe class="stem-frame" data-src="embeds/linkage.html?mode=four" title="Four-bar linkage"></iframe>

::: notes
The crank (blue) turns; the rocker (green) swings. The pink path is drawn by point **P** on the coupler: different points draw different curves. That's how a machine can move something along a shape that no single wheel could.

Try the buttons on the right:

- **Crank-rocker**: the usual one. The crank goes all the way round; the rocker swings.
- **Double-crank**: make the ground the shortest link, and *both* sides turn fully.
- **Double-rocker**: the coupler is shortest; the crank can only rock back and forth. Watch it hit its limit and turn back.
- **Parallelogram**: opposite links are equal, so the coupler stays level (like a pantograph, or a bike's derailleur).
- **Straight line**: Hoeken's linkage. P moves in an almost straight line for part of the turn, made only from turning links.

Then drag the sliders: what makes the crank stop turning fully?
:::

## Grashof's rule

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Add the **shortest** and the **longest** link.

- If that is **less than or equal to** the other two added together, at least one link can turn **all the way round**.
- If it is **more**, no link can turn all the way. Everything only rocks.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Example:** 1, 4, 3 and 3.5

shortest + longest = 1 + 4 = **5**

the other two = 3 + 3.5 = **6.5**

5 ≤ 6.5, so one link turns fully ✓
:::
::::

::: notes
The simulator checks this rule live, on the right, as you change the lengths. **Which** link turns fully depends on which link is the shortest: the crank (crank-rocker), the ground (double-crank) or the coupler (double-rocker: the coupler spins, but the crank and rocker only swing).
:::

## Will the crank turn all the way round?

::: {.sort}
- **Yes, it turns fully**
  - Crank 1, coupler 4, rocker 3, ground 3.5 | 1 + 4 = 5 ≤ 3 + 3.5 = 6.5, and the crank is the shortest link.
  - Crank 2, coupler 5, rocker 4, ground 4 | 2 + 5 = 7 ≤ 4 + 4 = 8, and the crank is the shortest link.
  - Crank 1.5, coupler 3, rocker 3, ground 2 | 1.5 + 3 = 4.5 ≤ 3 + 2 = 5, and the crank is the shortest link.
- **No, it only rocks**
  - Crank 3, coupler 3, rocker 3, ground 4 | 3 + 4 = 7 is more than 3 + 3 = 6: no link turns fully.
  - Crank 4, coupler 2, rocker 4, ground 5 | 2 + 5 = 7 ≤ 4 + 4 = 8, but the coupler is the shortest, so the crank only rocks.
  - Crank 3, coupler 5, rocker 2, ground 4.5 | 2 + 5 = 7 ≤ 3 + 4.5 = 7.5, but the rocker is the shortest: the rocker turns, not the crank.
:::

::: notes
Check any of these in the simulator: type the lengths in with the sliders and watch.
:::

## Six-bar linkages {#six-bar}

<iframe class="stem-frame" data-src="embeds/linkage.html?mode=watt" title="Six-bar linkage"></iframe>

::: notes
A **six-bar** adds two more links (orange) and a third ground pivot. The extra links let a machine do more with one motor: a bigger swing, a pause, or a more complicated path.

- **Watt** (shown first): two four-bars in a row. The rocker is a three-joint piece (the green triangle), and it drives the second four-bar.
- **Stephenson** (button at the top): the extra links hang from the path point P on the coupler, so F follows a new path.

Real six-bars: car suspensions, excavator buckets, many walking robots, and the legs of Theo Jansen's walking Strandbeest sculptures.
:::

## Name the links

::: {.matching}
- ground | The link that doesn't move
- crank | The link the motor turns
- coupler | The link that joins the two sides
- rocker | The link that swings back and forth
- joint | A pin where two links can turn
- coupler curve | The path a point on the coupler draws
:::

## Design your own

- **PMKS+**: design and test planar linkages in the browser, with paths, speeds and forces. [pmksplus.com](https://pmksplus.com){target="_blank"}
- **MotionGen**: draw linkages and make them follow a path you choose; free, on the web and on tablets. [motiongen.io](https://motiongen.io){target="_blank"}
- **Linkage** (free Windows program): quick sketches of linkages that move. [Linkage Mechanism Designer](https://blog.rectorsquid.com/linkage-mechanism-designer-and-simulator/){target="_blank"}
- **GeoGebra**: search "four-bar linkage" on geogebra.org for many ready-made models.

::: notes
These are outside tools (they need the internet). The simulator in this deck is saved in the course (`embeds/linkage.html`, built with JSXGraph), so it works offline.
:::
